answer.exemplar: Every conic with a centre has a point symmetry about it: a half turn around the centre maps each point of the curve to another point of the same curve. A centre can only be a symmetry point of a curve that has two axes of symmetry, because reflecting in one axis and then in the other is the same as the half turn, and neither reflection is available to a parabola, which has only one. The practical test is that the linear terms in the general equation must be removable by a translation alone, with no rotation. Completing the square in x and in y, and reading off the shifts, either produces a centre and the claim holds, or it leaves a term in a single variable, which is the fingerprint of a parabola and the disproof of the claim.
